name: power-law-behaviors
of: A mechanism by which a venture fund's arithmetic, its size, its fees, its carry, its reserves, its concentration cap, its term, and the quarterly letter that carries its marks, dictates how an investor behaves toward a founder at the table, named with the arithmetic, its carrier, the behavior it produces, and the founder-side move that exploits or defends against it, and sorted by whether the behavior would vanish if the fund were half its size or persists at any size because the money is other people's.
items: Below the care line: a check smaller than the fund's smallest meaningful position is priced by the fund as an option on seeing the next round rather than as an investment, as a two-billion-dollar fund's two-million-dollar seed cannot move its return whatever the company does; the carrier is the ratio of the check to the fund, the behavior is indifference, an associate in the board seat, no fight over terms and none for the company, and the founder's move is to take the money only as passive capital beside a lead whose fund the check is large enough to hurt; not the partner's inattention, which is a person, since the same partner cares at a fund a tenth the size, and the one behavior on the map that vanishes entirely when the fund is resized.

Table below the line: a round made only of checks that sit below each writer's own care line has no holder whose arithmetic makes it show up at the bridge, so the party round of twelve small checks is cheap and quick to raise and nobody's when the company needs a lead, a bridge, or a signature in a hurry; the carrier is the sum of ratios across the table rather than any one of them, the behavior is a cap table that goes silent at once, and the founder's move is to seat at least one holder for whom the position is large relative to its fund, even at a worse price, since that holder will do the work; not Below the care line, which is one indifferent check, since twelve indifferent checks make a second thing, a table with no seat, and it vanishes the moment any one check crosses its writer's line.

Fund on one exit: a fund that must return about three times its capital from one or two positions, after fees have eaten fifteen to twenty percent of it, requires of each company an exit that, at the ownership the fund will still hold after dilution, returns the whole fund, as a five-hundred-million-dollar fund holding ten percent at exit needs a five-billion-dollar sale; the carrier is the fund size divided by the ownership at exit, the behavior is the pass on a business that will very probably sell for three hundred million, delivered as 'not venture scale', and the founder's move is to raise from a fund whose size the plausible exit does return, since a fifty-million-dollar fund at ten percent is returned by five hundred million; not a judgment of odds, since the ninety-percent case is passed and the five-percent case is taken, and the threshold halves when the fund does.

Round sized from the far end: the fund's model fixes an ownership it must hold at exit and the dilution it expects between, so it fixes the ownership it must buy now, and its check size, fixed by fund size over the number of positions, then fixes the round, so a ten-million-dollar check at twenty percent is a fifty-million post-money whether or not the company needs ten million, and the fund asks the founder to 'raise a proper round' or to take the check at a lower price, counting its ownership net of the option pool the pre-money must carry; the carrier is the ownership target, the behavior is a round whose size was derived on the fund's side before the plan was read, and the founder's move is to learn the fund's check and target, back out the round it can say yes to, or split the target between two leads who each accept less; not Fund on one exit, which passes, since this one accepts and resizes, and the check halves with the fund while the target does not.

Silence of the one who could have: when a fund large enough to lead the next round takes a small position in this one, its later absence from the round is read by every outsider as knowledge, since the party with the most information and the most money declined, so the seed from the big fund carries a signal at the A that the same seed from a fund that never leads As cannot carry; the carrier is the insider's capacity relative to the round, the behavior is the outsider's question 'why isn't your seed investor leading', which the insider cannot answer without either leading or damning, and the founder's move is to take seed from funds too small to lead, or from a program the big fund has walled off by policy so that its silence is a rule rather than a verdict; not Pockets, not opinion, where the absence is arithmetic, since this absence is a choice, and the signal exists only where the fund is big enough to have had one.

Fund that grew away: management fees are a percentage of committed capital, so the partners' income doubles when the fund does, and the successor fund is sized by what the limited partners will give and what the fees need rather than by what the portfolio will need, so the fund that led the seed at fifty million has raised five hundred by the A and can no longer write a check the A can absorb at its ownership target; the carrier is the fee on committed capital, the behavior is the insider who cheers the company and cannot lead its next round, which then reads as the silence above, and the founder's move is to ask which fund the pro-rata will be drawn from and to read the insider's own fundraising as a forecast of who will be at the next table; contested as a critique of managers, kept here as arithmetic about which fund exists when the next round comes; not Below the care line, since this fund was the right size when it arrived and moved.

Living dead by denominator: after investment the fund sorts its portfolio by which companies can still return it, and a company that cannot is assigned no reserves and no partner time and is offered a quick sale, because a two-times return on a five-million-dollar check adds nothing to a half-billion fund while the sale frees a board seat and returns capital the fund may recycle into a fresh position, so the small early exit has a value to the fund unrelated to its multiple; the carrier is the reserve model and the recycling provision, the behavior is the conversation about 'finding a home', and the founder's move is to notice that the label lives in the denominator, since the same company is a fund-returner to a thirty-million-dollar fund, and to move the position to that fund by secondary, often below the last price, which frees the company and gives the seller the distribution it wanted; not Fund on one exit, which is run at entry, since this company was admitted, and the hinge of the map, since the label vanishes when the fund is halved and the triage does not.

Big holder wants the high price: on a round it partly funds, an investor's stake in the price has the sign of its existing position's value minus its new dollars, so a holder with twenty percent worth twenty million that puts four million into the round gains more on the letter from a higher price than it pays in the round and argues the price up, while the two-percent holder and the new lead argue it down; the carrier is the ratio of stake to new money, the behavior is the largest insider taking the founder's side on price at the bridge, and the founder's move is to read each holder's stance on price off the cap table before the meeting rather than off its faith in the company, and to let the big holder name the number the new money must meet; not generosity, and reversed the moment the round is large relative to the stake, as at a recapitalization, where the same holder wants the price down.

Stranger's price on the letter: a fund carries a position at the last round's price only when the price was set at arm's length, so a round priced by insiders alone marks little and a round led by an outsider marks the insider's whole position, which is why the insider that could fund the round by itself shops it to strangers and gives up allocation to get a stranger's number; the carrier is the fair-value rule the fund's auditor applies, the behavior is the insider distributing the deck and introducing the leads it will then compete with for allocation, and the founder's move is to take the insider's shopping as free distribution and to price the outsider's lead against the insider's need for the mark, since the insider will backstop the round to keep the stranger in; not what-a-price-does' Price for the stranger's eyes, where a seller protects a recorded number, since here a buyer procures a stranger to set one, and the item on which Big holder wants the high price depends, since a price nobody outside will sign at marks nothing.

Mark kept by structure: a fund's mark is made on the headline price and not on the preference-adjusted value, so a fund facing a down round prefers a flat price with a senior preference, a multiple, or a ratchet to a lower price with clean terms, because the letter records the price and the structure is invisible to it, and the founder's ownership drains through the preference stack at a price that never moved; the carrier is a valuation policy that reads price and not terms, the behavior is 'we can hold the valuation if we add some protection', and the founder's move is to price the structure as the down round it is, to take the clean lower price when the common's share of the plausible exits is higher under it, and to hear the insider's preference for structure as a statement about its letter and not about the company; adds to dilution-carriers' Headline bought with terms, which prices the trade, the investor's motive for it, a letter that cannot see the terms; not the preference itself, which is a term, and present at any fund size, since the letter is written for whoever's money it is.

Vintage's two appetites: a fund raises its successor on its marks two to four years in and on its distributions after, and is wound up at ten years plus extensions, so a young fund wants a priced up-round before its next raise and an old fund wants cash, and the same company hears 'raise more, go bigger' from one board seat and 'take the offer' from the other, each seat reading its own fund's calendar, as the whaling agent wanted the ship home with the oil while the captain wanted one more whale; the carrier is the term in the limited partnership agreement and the fundraising it forces, the behavior is a board split by vintage rather than by belief, and the founder's move is to read each investor's stance on the fork from its fund's age before asking, and to seat funds whose calendars agree; not tollgates-that-must-buy's Powder that must be lit, which is the compulsion to buy by a date, since this is what the fund needs to have happened to your company by when, and Sequoia's 2021 restructuring of its US and European business into an open-ended fund without a term removed exactly this behavior and no other on the map.

Call option at the board: carry is a share of profit above capital returned, a call option on the whole fund, so a fund whose portfolio is under water holds an option out of the money and wants variance, opposing the sale at one times that would return capital and pressing for the raise that might return the fund, while a fund already returned wants to lock in and supports the sale; the carrier is the moneyness of the carry, the behavior is a board seat's stance on the acquisition offer set by the rest of that fund's portfolio, which the founder never sees, and the founder's move is to ask how the fund is doing before asking what it thinks, and to expect the under-water fund to want the swing that a diversified holder would not; by analogy the whaling captain on a lay with an empty hold late in the voyage hunts the worse water; not Fund on one exit, which is applied at entry to a company, since this is applied at exit by a portfolio's state, and it does not move when the fund is halved.

Chips bought off the table: a founder holds one undiversified position and prefers the sure three hundred million, while the fund holds thirty and prefers the swing, so the fund buys the founder's risk aversion with cash, allowing or arranging a secondary sale of founder shares at the round so that the founder will refuse the acquisition the fund does not want; the carrier is the founder's concave utility set against the fund's near-linear one, the behavior is secondary offered exactly at the round where an offer might come, and the founder's move is to ask for it there, since it is the price of variance and the fund is the buyer; contested, since some funds hold that a founder with money stops swinging, so the same arithmetic produces the opposite policy at other tables, and the map keeps both as one mechanism with a disputed sign; not a liquidity event, since the cash is bought for what it does to the founder's next decision.

Orphan on the board: carry is divided among partners by attribution, and a partner's standing rides on the deals carried under their name inside their own promotion window, so a junior partner wants a visible markup by a brand-name lead before the partnership vote and will help the founder get one at a lower ownership, and when a partner leaves the company loses the one person in the reserve model whose carry it was, so the successor, who gets no credit for it, lets it drift into the living dead regardless of its numbers; the carrier is the attribution of carry and the partner's clock inside the fund's, the behavior is a company whose treatment changes on a personnel move nobody at the company made, and the founder's move is to negotiate a named successor with attribution on departure, or to buy the position out; adjacent to deal-deaths' Champion's single-tender want, which kills a deal before signing, since this changes the treatment of a company already owned.

Cap that sells the winner: the partnership agreement caps any one position at ten to twenty percent of the fund, so the fund cannot keep buying its best company past the cap and must watch the rounds it wants most go to outsiders or to a second vehicle it raises for the purpose, which then must price a round its own first fund also holds; the carrier is the concentration limit written by the limited partners, the behavior is a fund that fights for super pro-rata in the middling companies and cannot take pro-rata in the good one, and a fund that arrives with an opportunity fund and an appetite above its rights, and the founder's move is to run the second vehicle's appetite as competitive tension for the outside lead's price; not a reserve shortage, since the money exists and the rule forbids it, and it does not move when the fund is halved, since the cap is a fraction.

Pockets, not opinion: reserves are allocated per company from a finite pool, and a fund whose reserves are spent, on other companies or on this one in an earlier bridge, cannot take its pro-rata, so its absence from the round looks like the silence of the one who could have while being arithmetic, and the fund usually will not say so, since 'we are out of reserves' is heard by its other companies and by its next fund's investors; the carrier is the reserve ledger, the behavior is an unexplained absence that kills the round, and the founder's move is to make the ledger visible by asking the fund to sell or assign its pro-rata right to a co-investor or a special-purpose vehicle, which is the one act that says out of money rather than out of faith; adds to term-sheet-powers' Reserves test in loyalty's clothing, which sorts the syndicate by reserves, and its Option on the next round's information, which prices the right, the fund's motive for silence and the assignment as the founder's cure; not Silence of the one who could have, since the tell cures this one, and the last stop before the fund's money reaches zero.

Vote without a checkbook: a fund that cannot raise a successor keeps its board seats, protective provisions, and pro-rata rights while its fees step down and its partners leave, so it can block a down round that would write its mark down and a sale below its carrying value, and can neither lead, follow, nor bridge; the carrier is the paper that outlives the money, the behavior is a veto from a seat that can no longer buy, and the founder's move is a secondary purchase of the zombie's position, which it often sells below the mark because any distribution is the one thing its limited partners still want, or a round structured so that its consent is not required; adds to dilution-carriers' Veto without votes, which is the provision, the fund state in which the provision is all the fund has left; not a fund that is merely slow, and the far endpoint of the map, the behavior that remains when the fund's money is halved and halved again to nothing, since what remains is the agreement.

source.register: Operator-grade and concrete: fund sizes over ownership at exit, reserve ledgers, concentration caps, fair-value marks, carry moneyness, partner attribution, pro-rata assignments; drawn from venture practice with the whaling voyage as the one remote case.
source.mode: Analytical mechanisms with stylized illustrative arithmetic (two-and-twenty, a ten-year term, a three-times target) and observed cases simplified to one mechanism each; two items (Fund that grew away, Chips bought off the table) carry contested modality and say so, and the whaling captain is an analogy.
source.via: practice-deep-ideonomy; two Fable fieldwork breaths; independent Fable editorial review
boundary_claim: Authored analytical fieldwork with stylized arithmetic (two-and-twenty, a ten-year term, a three-times target, a ten-to-twenty-percent cap); real funds vary, and a real behavior at a table usually has several of these arithmetics behind it at once.

The seriation is an itinerary from behaviors that vanish when the fund is resized to behaviors that persist at any size, not a ranking of importance; its far pole is really 'intrinsic to a closed-end fund that writes a quarterly letter', and an evergreen or corporate vehicle removes some of it, as the Sequoia case shows for one item.

The illustrative cases (the whaling lay, the signaling discourse around big-fund seeds, the 2021 open-ended restructuring) are simplified to one mechanism each and the whaling captain is an analogy, not a claim about whaling history.

Two items carry contested modality: Fund that grew away is a critique of managers kept only as arithmetic about which fund exists at the next round, and Chips bought off the table has a disputed sign that practitioners resolve both ways.

Limited-partner behaviors (defaults on capital calls, sales of fund interests), corporate and sovereign investors without carry or a term, and the tactical use of the absent principal ('my LPs won't allow it') are outside the map.

seriation.axis: What the behavior is a function of: from the fund's size relative to your check and your round, so that resizing the fund removes it, through ratios inside the cap table that fund size does not touch, to the fund's state under other people's money (the letter, the term, the carry, the cap, the reserve ledger, the agreement), which persists as the money is halved and halved again to nothing.
seriation.note: An authored itinerary, not a scalar of importance or of harm. Below the care line opens it because it is the only behavior that vanishes outright when the fund is resized; Table below the line, Fund on one exit, Round sized from the far end, Silence of the one who could have, and Fund that grew away follow as behaviors whose threshold, check, signal, or successor scales with the fund. Living dead by denominator is the hinge: the label (living dead, fund-returner) moves with the denominator and vanishes when the fund is halved, while the triage that acts on the label (no reserves, no time, find a home) is partner time and recycling, which no resizing removes, so one item straddles the two halves and the edge from it to Fund on one exit is the founder's way to cross. Big holder wants the high price follows as the first behavior that fund size cannot touch, since its ratio is stake to new money. The second half, Stranger's price on the letter through Vote without a checkbook, runs by which piece of other people's money carries the behavior: the letter's valuation rule (Stranger's price, Mark kept by structure), the term (Vintage's two appetites), the carry (Call option at the board, Chips bought off the table, Orphan on the board), the limited partners' cap (Cap that sells the winner), the reserve ledger (Pockets, not opinion), and finally the bare agreement (Vote without a checkbook), which closes the walk because it is what remains at size zero. Pockets, not opinion → Vote without a checkbook is the consequential adjacency: the same absence is a curable fact about one company on one side and a standing veto about the whole fund on the other, and the founder's move changes kind, from asking for a letter to buying the seat.

relations.label: If the partner whose carry the company was leaves, then the company enters the triage with no advocate in the reserve model, so the denominator test is run against it by someone with nothing to gain from passing it, and numbers that would have kept it alive under its sponsor no longer do.

exploration.first_question: By what mechanisms does a venture fund's arithmetic (its size, its fees, its carry, its reserves, its term) dictate how a partner behaves toward a founder at the table, and what does each behavior let the founder do?
exploration.changed_question: Which of these behaviors are functions of the fund's size relative to the company, so that a fund half the size would not produce them, and which are functions of the fund's state under other people's money, a letter, a term, a carry, a cap, a ledger, an agreement, so that no resizing removes them? The first breath put every behavior at the round, in the price, the size, and the pass; sharpening reserves against the zombie showed that the most consequential behaviors happen between rounds and at the exit, and come from the fund's state, its moneyness, its age, its ledger, its partner's tenure, rather than its size.
exploration.new_member: Call option at the board: carry is a share of profit above capital returned, a call option on the whole fund, so a fund whose portfolio is under water holds an option out of the money and wants variance, opposing the sale at one times that would return capital and pressing for the raise that might return the fund, while a fund already returned wants to lock in and supports the sale; the carrier is the moneyness of the carry, the behavior is a board seat's stance on the acquisition offer set by the rest of that fund's portfolio, which the founder never sees, and the founder's move is to ask how the fund is doing before asking what it thinks, and to expect the under-water fund to want the swing that a diversified holder would not; by analogy the whaling captain on a lay with an empty hold late in the voyage hunts the worse water; not Fund on one exit, which is applied at entry to a company, since this is applied at exit by a portfolio's state, and it does not move when the fund is halved.

priorities.item: Big holder wants the high price: on a round it partly funds, an investor's stake in the price has the sign of its existing position's value minus its new dollars, so a holder with twenty percent worth twenty million that puts four million into the round gains more on the letter from a higher price than it pays in the round and argues the price up, while the two-percent holder and the new lead argue it down; the carrier is the ratio of stake to new money, the behavior is the largest insider taking the founder's side on price at the bridge, and the founder's move is to read each holder's stance on price off the cap table before the meeting rather than off its faith in the company, and to let the big holder name the number the new money must meet; not generosity, and reversed the moment the round is large relative to the stake, as at a recapitalization, where the same holder wants the price down.
priorities.why: It is a sign computed from two numbers every founder already has, and it predicts a stance most founders get backwards, so it can be tested on paper against any bridge round that has minutes.
priorities.next_question: Take five bridge or extension rounds from the last two years where each holder's position on price is on record; for each holder compute the value of its existing stake at the old price minus the new dollars it will put in, predict its stance on price from the sign, and count the misses; a miss rate under one in five makes the cap table a better predictor of the price argument than anyone's faith in the company.

priorities.item: Living dead by denominator: after investment the fund sorts its portfolio by which companies can still return it, and a company that cannot is assigned no reserves and no partner time and is offered a quick sale, because a two-times return on a five-million-dollar check adds nothing to a half-billion fund while the sale frees a board seat and returns capital the fund may recycle into a fresh position, so the small early exit has a value to the fund unrelated to its multiple; the carrier is the reserve model and the recycling provision, the behavior is the conversation about 'finding a home', and the founder's move is to notice that the label lives in the denominator, since the same company is a fund-returner to a thirty-million-dollar fund, and to move the position to that fund by secondary, often below the last price, which frees the company and gives the seller the distribution it wanted; not Fund on one exit, which is run at entry, since this company was admitted, and the hinge of the map, since the label vanishes when the fund is halved and the triage does not.
priorities.why: Low plausibility that anyone builds it and high generative promise: if the label lives in the denominator, then a fund whose whole business is buying living-dead positions from big funds and leading their next rounds is a lead investor that never competes for a new deal, and its existence would be a test of the map's hinge.
priorities.next_question: List twenty secondary sales of a single venture position from a fund over five hundred million to a fund under one hundred million; record the price against the last round and whether the buyer then led the company's next round; if the buyer led in most cases at a price below the seller's mark, the denominator arbitrage exists and the hinge holds.

gate.standard: declared type, close-neighbor discriminator, boundary case, and form inference

neighbors.left: Silence of the one who could have: when a fund large enough to lead the next round takes a small position in this one, its later absence from the round is read by every outsider as knowledge, since the party with the most information and the most money declined, so the seed from the big fund carries a signal at the A that the same seed from a fund that never leads As cannot carry; the carrier is the insider's capacity relative to the round, the behavior is the outsider's question 'why isn't your seed investor leading', which the insider cannot answer without either leading or damning, and the founder's move is to take seed from funds too small to lead, or from a program the big fund has walled off by policy so that its silence is a rule rather than a verdict; not Pockets, not opinion, where the absence is arithmetic, since this absence is a choice, and the signal exists only where the fund is big enough to have had one.
neighbors.right: Pockets, not opinion: reserves are allocated per company from a finite pool, and a fund whose reserves are spent, on other companies or on this one in an earlier bridge, cannot take its pro-rata, so its absence from the round looks like the silence of the one who could have while being arithmetic, and the fund usually will not say so, since 'we are out of reserves' is heard by its other companies and by its next fund's investors; the carrier is the reserve ledger, the behavior is an unexplained absence that kills the round, and the founder's move is to make the ledger visible by asking the fund to sell or assign its pro-rata right to a co-investor or a special-purpose vehicle, which is the one act that says out of money rather than out of faith; adds to term-sheet-powers' Reserves test in loyalty's clothing, which sorts the syndicate by reserves, and its Option on the next round's information, which prices the right, the fund's motive for silence and the assignment as the founder's cure; not Silence of the one who could have, since the tell cures this one, and the last stop before the fund's money reaches zero.
neighbors.separating_case: The same absence from the same round from two insiders. A two-billion-dollar fund with untouched reserves that took the seed and does not lead the A: nothing the founder can produce cures it, since the fund's absence is a choice and the only cure was a policy the fund set before the seed. A sixty-million-dollar fund that bridged this company twice and has nothing left: its absence is a ledger fact, and the founder cures it by getting the fund to assign its pro-rata right to a co-investor, which no fund with money and doubt would do. One absence is cured by the fund's public policy, the other by its public ledger, and a fund cannot fake the second cure without giving up the right.

checks.boundary_case: 'My limited partners would never allow it' is the tempting nonmember: it is other people's money at its purest, and it is out, because it works as a bargaining shield whether or not any arithmetic stands behind it, so it is an authority tactic and belongs with the ratifier in deal-deaths and with negotiation lists, not here. The constraints the limited partners actually wrote that produce behavior by arithmetic, the concentration cap and the term, are in as Cap that sells the winner and Vintage's two appetites.
checks.form_inference: The map shows a loop the itinerary conceals, Round sized from the far end → Fund that grew away: the ownership target sizes the round, the round's size justifies the successor fund's size, and the successor's check needs a larger round, so the company's need is an input nowhere in the cycle. It shows a fork at Vintage's two appetites → Call option at the board: an old fund in the money wants your sale and an old fund under water wants your swing, so the vintage, which the sequence presents as one appetite per age, does not predict the vote without the moneyness. It shows two dependencies: Stranger's price on the letter → Big holder wants the high price, where the holder's price preference is worth nothing until an outsider signs, and Orphan on the board → Living dead by denominator, where the triage depends on who is left to argue. It shows an incompatibility at Cap that sells the winner → Big holder wants the high price: past the cap a fund can keep the mark or the ownership, not both. It shows a passage between levels at Pockets, not opinion → Vote without a checkbook, where an absence about one company becomes a veto about the whole fund and the founder's move changes kind. And the edge Living dead by denominator → Fund on one exit is the live question drawn: the one place where halving the fund, by moving the position to a fund half the size, changes a behavior after the fact.
checks.target_preserved: Self-read only. Each item names an arithmetic, a carrier, a behavior at the table, and a founder-side move, and the strange members are kept as mechanisms rather than softened into advice: the largest holder as the founder's ally on price, the fund that cannot buy more of its best company, a letter that is paid in mark for structure the founder pays for, a veto from a seat with no money, and a secondary sale that reruns the fund-returner test with a smaller denominator. Two contested items keep their modality visible rather than being dropped for safety.
